bib.title: One Small Step for Generative AI, One Giant Leap for AGI: A Complete Survey on ChatGPT in AIGC Era

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "One Small Step for Generative AI, One Giant Leap for AGI: A Complete Survey on ChatGPT in AIGC Era", Chaoning Zhang et al. (16 authors; Kyung Hee Univ., KAIST and others). arXiv:2304.06488v1 [cs.CY], 4 Apr 2023. Marked "Manuscript submitted to ACM" (ACM format, "© 2022", "1, 1 (April 2022)"), so it is an unreviewed preprint. The ACM date of 2022 is a template error. File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/01-llm-fundamentals/sources/zhang-2023-one-small-step-generative-ai.pdf

COVERAGE: 117,522 of 117,522 chars extracted from all 29 pages. Everything before the references was read in full. References (about pp. 22-29, roughly 226 entries) were skimmed only, not read in detail. The text extracted cleanly. Page numbers below are PDF pages.

VERDICT: This is a low-depth, early-2023 survey. For a LLM-fundamentals note it adds almost nothing that is not better sourced from the primary papers. The technology section is about 4 pages. The rest is applications, misuse and ethics. It can sharpen two or three timeline or definition statements and serve as a "what people believed in April 2023" snapshot. Several of its own numbers are secondhand or wrong, and these are flagged below.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: GPT-1 through GPT-3 sizes. GPT-1 is decoder-only, 12 layers, 117M parameters, trained on BooksCorpus. GPT-2 has 1.5B parameters and 8M web pages. GPT-3 has 175B parameters, 96 attention layers and a 3.2M batch size.
  number: 117M; 1.5B; 175B; 96 layers; 3.2M batch
  setup: descriptive of the OpenAI papers (the survey cites the GPT-1, GPT-2 and GPT-3 papers), not new measurement. The 3.2M batch is a token-count figure in the GPT-3 paper; the survey does not say what unit it uses.
  quote: "GPT-1 adopts a 12-layer Transformer and has 117M parameters"; "GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters, 96 attention layers, and a 3.2 M batch size"
  where: p.8
- claim: GPT-1 beat task-specific models on 9 of 12 tasks. GPT-2 reached state of the art zero-shot on 7 of 8 language-modelling datasets but did poorly on question answering.
  number: 9 of 12; 7 of 8
  setup: figures from the original GPT-1 and GPT-2 papers; GPT-2 in the zero-shot setting.
  quote: "outperforms models trained for specific tasks in 9 of 12 tasks"; "GPT-2 achieved state-of-the-art results on 7 of 8 language modeling datasets tested"
  where: p.8
- claim: Table 1 gives the GPT vs BERT contrast. Both use attention Transformers, self-supervised learning and fine-tuning. GPT is unidirectional, decoder-only and autoregressive. BERT is bidirectional, encoder-only and uses masked language modelling. The survey says BERT is rarely used downstream without finetuning, while autoregressive models do few-shot and zero-shot generation.
  number: none
  quote: "GPT uses unidirectional text context, while BERT uses bidirectional text context."; "BERT is rarely used for the downstream task without finetuning"
  where: p.7-8
- claim: GPT-4 was released on March 14, 2023 as a multimodal model taking text and images as input and giving text output. Human-level on professional exams but weaker in the real world. A simulated bar exam put it in the top 10% of takers, against the lowest 10% for GPT-3.5. Human raters preferred GPT-4 over GPT-3.5 on 70.2% of 5,214 prompts. Pre-training data ends September 2021.
  number: 14 Mar 2023; top 10% vs bottom 10%; 70.2% of 5,214; Sept 2021
  setup: secondhand from the GPT-4 report and OpenAI material (refs [122], [125], [77]). The setup is not given, such as who the raters were or which exam version. The 70.2% figure is a preference on OpenAI API and ChatGPT prompts, not a benchmark score.
  quote: "The answers by GPT-4 were favored over the responses produced by GPT-3.5 on 70.2% of the 5,214 questions in the sample provided to ChatGPT and the OpenAI API."; "the virtual bar exam result for GPT-4 is in the top 10% of test participants, as opposed to the score for GPT-3.5, which was in the lowest 10%"
  where: p.9
- claim: ChatGPT is described as a fine-tuned GPT-3.5. GPT-3.5 adds supervised finetuning and RLHF on top of GPT-3 (Fig. 5). The survey gives RLHF as the way to overcome the limits of learning only from unlabeled or labeled data. Its description of RLHF is loose: it lists "changing model parameters" as a form of human feedback.
  number: none
  quote: "GPT-3.5 is a variation of the widely popular GPT-3 and the ChatGPT is a fine-tuned version of GPT-3.5."
  where: p.9
- claim: ChatGPT passed 100M monthly active users within two months of its November 2022 release. It cites a news article, not a measurement.
  number: 100 million users in 2 months
  quote: "the number of active monthly users surpassed 100 million within only two months, breaking the user growth record of other social products [118]"
  where: p.4
- claim: OpenAI timeline and business figures as of early 2023. Founded December 11, 2015. Reorganised as for-profit in 2019. Microsoft was reported in talks to put in up to $10B. The Wall Street Journal valued OpenAI at about $29B. These are news-sourced and have dated.
  number: 11 Dec 2015; 2019; $10B; $29B
  quote: "Semafor claimed that Microsoft was in discussions to spend up to $10 billion [101]. According to the Wall Street Journal, OpenAI is worth roughly $29 billion [13]."
  where: p.4-5
- claim: A hallucination figure. A test asked for 10 groundbreaking medical papers with DOIs, five times. Only 8 of the 50 DOIs existed.
  number: 8 of 50 DOIs
  setup: single study [59] on ChatGPT, early 2023, medical domain. The survey does not name the model version.
  quote: "out of the 50 DOIs provided, only 8 of them exist and have been correctly published"
  where: p.11
- claim: The survey groups ChatGPT's limits as incorrect, illogical, inconsistent (sensitive to the prompt) and unconscious. It attributes incorrectness to training that mimics human demonstrators, which gives plausible-sounding answers at the cost of correctness.
  number: none
  quote: "the model mimics the human demonstrator to be plausible-sounding but often at the cost of correctness"
  where: p.16-17
- claim: Exam and application results quoted from other studies, all early 2023 and mostly ChatGPT (GPT-3.5). Only the TUCE, law-exam and USMLE results below were tested on whole exams. The rest are small studies.
  number: TUCE 63.3% micro, 86.7% macro; four Univ. of Minnesota law exams (95 multiple-choice, 12 essay questions) passed at C+; physics essays 71±2% vs module average 71±5%; clinical vignettes 71.7% over 36 cases; 39 of 45 vignettes (87%) correct in the top three vs 51% for symptom checkers; ACR imaging worst-case 56.25%
  setup: single-paper results, not replicated here. Sample sizes, prompts and model versions are not given beyond those counts.
  quote: "ChatGPT properly answers 63.3% of the microeconomics questions and 86.7% of the macroeconomics questions"; "ChatGPT achieved an overall accuracy of 71.7% across all the published clinical cases"; "The study reveals that ChatGPT passed all four courses and performed at the level of a C+ student."
  where: p.13-15
- claim: Labour-market exposure. One cited study puts 32.8% of jobs fully affected and 36.5% partly. OpenAI's own study finds at least 10% of tasks affected for 80% of US workers, and at least 50% of tasks for 19% of workers. The survey says high-wage jobs, such as lawyers, are at higher risk.
  number: 32.8%; 36.5%; 10% of tasks for 80%; 50% of tasks for 19%
  quote: "at least 10% of tasks for 80% of the US workforce and at least 50% of tasks for 19% of workers will be impacted"
  where: p.21
- claim: Student-use poll (Study.com, adult students) as cited: 89% used ChatGPT for homework, 48% for an at-home test or quiz, and 22% for a paper outline.
  number: 89%; 48%; 22%
  quote: "89% of them utilized ChatGPT for homework, and 48% of them exploited it for an at-home test or quiz"
  where: p.13
- claim: Pricing in early 2023. ChatGPT Plus was $20 a month against $30 for Grammarly Premium. ChatGPT was over 10 times slower than DeepL in a proofreading comparison.
  number: $20/month; $30/month; 10x slower
  quote: "Grammarly Premium, requires users to pay a monthly fee of $30, which is relatively more expensive compared to ChatGPT Plus's monthly fee of $20"
  where: p.12
- claim: The outlook proposes two roadmaps toward general-purpose AIGC. Roadmap 1 combines ChatGPT with other AIGC tools. Roadmap 2 is an all-in-one model. It notes GPT-4 takes images but outputs only text. These are speculation, not findings.
  number: none
  quote: "ChatGPT mainly excels at text-to-text tasks"; "Road-map 2: All-in-one strategy"
  where: p.20-21
- claim: GPT-4's report disclosed no technical details. Table 2 lists GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 parameters and data as "N.A."
  number: none
  quote: "providing no technical details on how these are achieved"; "N.A. indicates that there is no public disclosure."
  where: p.10, p.19

LIMITS
- The source's Table 2 data sizes look wrong, so do not copy them. It prints "BooksCorpus(over 40GB)", "WebText(40TB)" and "CommonCrawl (45TB)". These conflict with the cited papers as I recall them, roughly 5GB for BooksCorpus and 40GB for WebText. That is memory, not read from this PDF. Treat the table as unreliable unless checked against the primary papers.
- The survey is a literature digest of preprints and news up to early April 2023. It runs no experiments. It gives no training-cost, compute or token-count figures, and no scaling-law content.
- It does not cover GPT-3.5/InstructGPT RLHF mechanics beyond a figure reference. It does not cover tokenization, context windows (only "higher maximum token limit"), sampling, or alignment methods beyond one sentence.
- The authors concede ChatGPT's applications work is "still at the beginning" and that GPT-4 is not general-purpose AIGC. Most exam results come from the ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) era and have dated. The 500+ articles figure ("no fewer than 500") is a Google Scholar count from early 2023.
- Page 4 (Fig. 2) and Fig. 3 are images with no data in the text.

BUILDS ON: Vaswani et al. 2017 (Transformer, "Attention is All You Need" [182]); Radford et al. 2018 (GPT-1 [136]); Radford et al. 2019 (GPT-2 [137]); Brown et al. 2020 (GPT-3 [18]); OpenAI 2023 (GPT-4 report [122]); Devlin et al. (BERT [40/41]); Ouyang et al. (the Fig. 5 source, [125]; RLHF); Bengio, Ducharme and Vincent 2000 (neural probabilistic language model [11], for autoregressive modelling). The reference numbers come from the printed list; I did not check the full reference list entry by entry.

CODE: none. The only formulas are eq. (1) Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V and eq. (2) the autoregressive factorisation p(x)=p(x1)p(x2|x1)...p(xn|x1..x(n-1)), both on p.6-7. They are standard and need no source.

FIGURES
- Fig. 3 (p.8), "Timeline of GPT model families". Only useful as a one-glance timeline, and it is an image, so check it directly.
- Fig. 5 (p.10), "How GPT-3.5 is trained. Image obtained from [125]". It shows the supervised finetuning plus RLHF pipeline. The original, from the InstructGPT paper, is the better citation.
- Fig. 6 (p.20), "Roadmaps for bridging the gap between ChatGPT and AGI". Illustrates the two proposed routes. Speculative.
- Fig. 4 (p.9) shows the GPT-1 architecture and fine-tuning input transformations, taken from [136].
- Fig. 1 (p.3) is the survey structure overview; Fig. 2 (p.5) is the OpenAI products timeline. Low value.
I did not run the figures script; captions come from the extracted text. The text refers to the GPT timeline as both "Figure 6" and Fig. 3, so figure numbering in the source is inconsistent.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF text.
- A stale file /tmp/zh.txt from an earlier run held text from a different paper (arXiv 2311.07989, a code-LLM survey). Because of that, I discarded my first read and re-extracted into /tmp/zhang_real.txt. All claims above come from the re-extraction of this PDF only. The earlier mix-up is not a fault in the PDF.
- Internal inconsistencies: "ACM Reference Format" says 2022; the abstract says "more than 500 articles"; the text says "no fewer than 500". The abstract says GPT-4 is "a.k.a. ChatGPT plus", which is loose usage. The survey also calls the current ChatGPT "GPT-3" in Roadmap 1.
- Typos and loose wording, such as "the final authors" and "TOW ARDS AGI". None affect the numbers.

NOTE FOR CALLER: it adds nothing a note can use beyond a citation row for early-2023 context (GPT-1 to GPT-4 timeline, the 100M-users-in-two-months claim, the GPT vs BERT table). For parameter or data facts, cite the primary papers. Per the repo rule, file it as "sharpens" for any note that already covers GPT-1 to GPT-3 sizes or the BERT/GPT contrast.
